title: First Reported Case of Lorazepam-Assisted Interview in a Young Indian Female Presenting with Dissociative Identity Disorder and Improvement in Symptoms after the Interview
case_prompt: A 16-year-old unmarried Kashmiri schoolgirl was referred for a 5-month history of complete loss of personal memory. She did not recognize her name, parents, school friends, or basic academic knowledge expected of a 10th-grade student. She was unable to perform previously mastered skills such as playing computer videogames. Attendants noted regressive behaviors, including thumb sucking and childlike speech. She denied any history of trauma, sexual abuse, head injury, loss of consciousness, seizures, mania, psychosis, or substance use. Past medical, psychiatric, family, and social histories were unremarkable. On examination, she was cooperative, appropriately dressed, and described her mood as euthymic. Thinking was goal directed; she had no delusions, hallucinations, derealization, or thought disorder. She was oriented to time, place, and person, with intact attention, concentration, and memory on immediate testing, but she could not recall her name, home address, or life events preceding admission and confabulated when pressed. She lacked insight and appeared unconcerned. Physical and neurological examinations were normal. EEG, brain MRI, basic laboratory tests, and toxicology screen showed no abnormalities. The Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES) score was 50%. A DES score of ≥48% is indicative of dissociative identity disorder. Based on the history, mental-status examination, and high DES score, a diagnosis of dissociative identity disorder was made, and she was admitted for further management.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Organic neurological disorder was excluded — “Neurological assessment and basic laboratory testing including electroencephalography (EEG), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and drug screening revealed no significant abnormalities.”  
2. Seizure disorder was unlikely — “There were no symptoms suggestive of seizure …”  
3. Substance intoxication or withdrawal was excluded — “She never drank alcohol or abused any psychoactive substances.”  
4. Psychotic disorder was ruled out — “She had no delusions/hallucinations/derealisation/thought disorders.”  
5. Dementia was unlikely given preserved orientation and cognition — “She was oriented to time, place, and person with intact attention and concentration …”  
6. Dissociative amnesia or fugue was less consistent — “In dissociative amnesia, there is sudden loss of memory for a variable period of time … without any central nervous system (CNS) disease” and “the regression to a younger state was not consistent with simple DA or transient childish fugue identity in DA, as there was continuous change in personality and not remembering her biodata for 6 months.”  
7. Dissociative identity disorder was supported by chronic identity fragmentation and a high screening score — “Further score of 48% or above is indicative of diagnosis of DID .”
